articles.summary: University of Ottawa's president is acknowledging "a failure of the university" as Indigenous academics go public with allegations that a difficult work environment, poor treatment and racism at…

image.caption: A plaque outside University of Ottawa's Tabaret Hall discusses its founding in 1848 by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate as a bilingual Catholic college. (Brett Forester/CBC)

blocks.text: Indigenous academics say a difficult work environment, poor treatment and racism at the University of Ottawa, and a lack of effort to address those problems, has led multiple promising Indigenous scholars to quit.

In interviews, seven current and former uOttawa professors spoke negatively of their experience at the university, with some saying the institution has yet to reckon with its own history of training Catholic priests to run residential schools. Others blamed modern governance issues like a lack of Indigenous representation among senior leadership and a failure to address complaints.

In a year-long investigation, CBC Indigenous learned of an unresolved racism grievance filed by professors Veldon Coburn and Pierrot Ross-Tremblay, the exodus of seven Indigenous faculty members across multiple departments in one year starting in 2023, a civil lawsuit filed by one of them after leaving, and the early retirement of one long-serving Métis professor who called himself "a wounded soldier" and the environment "toxic."

The latest person to leave and speak out is Coburn, a member of the Algonquins of Pikwàkanagàn who officially resigned this summer, echoing a sentiment that the incidents are not isolated but a pattern.
"In the end, it was just a fairly pathetic attempt by the administration to have an Algonquin token, that there was never any real effort," Coburn said of his experience.
Though the university officially recognizes it sits on traditional unceded Algonquin territory, there was no attempt to retain him or resolve his complaint, which remains active, Coburn said.
Veldon Coburn is now an associate professor and faculty chair of the Indigenous Relations Initiative at McGill University in Montreal. (McGill University)
"In fact, it was just a record of poor treatment that is reflective of the larger relationship that the institution has with the Algonquin nation."

In a sit-down interview at her office, university president and vice-chancellor Marie-Eve Sylvestre called the complaints "a reminder that we have so much more to do" and personally committed to doing better.

"I see this as a failure of the university for having been unable to create an inclusive and respectful environment, and I want to make sure that we put in place the conditions to do better in the future," said Sylvestre, a former law faculty dean who became president in 2025.
Marie-Eve Sylvestre is president and vice-chancellor at University of Ottawa and was previously dean of the civil law section at the university's faculty of law. (Brett Forester/CBC)
"Universities are colonial institutions … especially us at the University of Ottawa, given that we were founded by the Oblates," she said.
"We are investigating our past at the moment, and we are sponsoring a history project into the connections between the University of Ottawa and the residential school system."

The president's comments acknowledge concerns that have been circulating. From its founding until 1965 the university was administered by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a Catholic order that ran 46 residential schools.
Oblates founded university

Its most notorious known alumnus may be bishop Jules Leguerrier, who obtained a theology degree in 1942 and went on to be the principal at St. Anne's residential school in northern Ontario from 1944 to 1975. Children at the school were subject to extreme physical and sexual abuse and Leguerrier allegedly physically assaulted children including by whipping them and using a homemade electric chair.
Some feel this colonial history casts a long shadow.
"It's part of your history, of your faculty and education. You have to recognize this history," said Nancy Wiscutie-Crépeau.
Wiscutie-Crépeau, who is Anicinabe from Senneterre in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region of Quebec, quit after a stint in the faculty of education's French sector.

items: Police hunted for secret church archives during probe of abuse allegations at St. Anne's residential school
St. Anne's residential school horrors revealed by police files

blocks.text: She told CBC Indigenous she remains bitter and angry about her experience, describing the environment as colonial and disappointing.
"I can't say if there is racism, but what I know is that there is a profound lack of knowledge about Indigenous people," she said in French.
"There is a deep, I would say, ignorance of who we are."

Tricia McGuire-Adams, a member of Bingwi Neyaashi Anishinaabek in northern Ontario, left the education faculty at around the same time in 2023. She spent four years there starting in 2019 but said she "experienced really harmful anti-Indigenous racism" and is now much happier at the University of Toronto.
"I chose to leave because the microaggressions became too heavy," McGuire-Adams said.

"My health began to suffer, my mental health began to suffer. My connection to community and my family began to suffer. And so I know that if I had chosen to stay, I would have continued to deteriorate on that health level."
Another First Nations former professor sued the university in 2023 for $1.4 million over an incident of alleged inappropriate sexual contact.

The statement of claim says the professor "made every effort to seek a resolution" but that "it was clear the University of Ottawa would not take steps to rectify or remediate the situation." The professor was "forced to seek employment at another university," according to the statement of claim.
The allegations are untested in court, no defences were filed, and it's unclear how the case was resolved.
Some professors cited the handling of that case with concern, while one person said the departure of Métis scholar Larry Chartrand was also eyebrow-raising and noteworthy.
'A wounded soldier'

Chartrand worked as a celebrated law professor at uOttawa for nearly 30 years, joining the university in 1994. In a phone interview, he described a slow process of disillusionment and frustration that led him to retire early in 2019.

"I kind of lost faith in the law," Chartrand said, "but also after you butt heads with the institution about Indigenous reform for so long, you kind of want to just say, OK, that's enough. I'm a wounded soldier. I think I'm going to retire."
He said it would be accurate to say the environment at uOttawa is difficult and colonial, even toxic.
"We're only learning now actually how toxic it can be as an Indigenous prof teaching, for example, the laws that tell you you're inferior," he said.
"It's kind of like being in a residential school in there, but you're the one doing the teaching. And yeah, it can be very troubling."

Chartrand said the university's status as an officially bilingual university with a legal mandate to preserve and develop francophone culture in Ontario can create friction and competition with Indigenous initiatives.

Another former professor, who requested confidentiality out of fears of professional reprisal, blamed this state of affairs on an internal glass ceiling and a failure to promptly address grievances like Coburn's or the one raised in the lawsuit.
"There's like a hopelessness, and you feel like you've exhausted all of your options and it's still not resolved," the person said.
"There's something systemically problematic happening if all these people are leaving all at once, and it doesn't look good."
University of Ottawa's Tabaret Hall circa 1920. The university became a provincially funded secular institution in 1965. (Canada. Dept. of Interior/Library and Archives Canada/PA-034331)

Echoing that, Darren O'Toole, who is Métis and a current uOttawa law associate professor, said a veteran scholar like Chartrand's retirement raised concerns that subsequent departures only reinforced.
"It's atrocious," O'Toole said.
"I mean University of Ottawa at this point, it'd be a sort of revolving door for Indigenous faculty."
O'Toole, who is supporting Coburn and Ross-Tremblay in their grievance, said Indigenous studies professors are isolated in a red brick former nunnery that looks like a residential school.
"In terms of a toxic culture, if you're sort of isolated like that, don't have contacts with members in other departments in that, you don't realize that it's not normal," he said.
Amir Attaran, who is not Indigenous but is seconded as legal counsel for the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation Tribal Council, is also speaking out in support of Indigenous faculty.
"I come from the United States. I have never experienced systemic racism as bad as I've seen at the University of Ottawa," Attaran said in an interview.
President responds
During the interview at her office, uOttawa president Sylvestre said she is aware of most of the cases but cannot comment on them specifically for confidentiality and privacy reasons.
Speaking generally, Sylvestre said the university has had its "ups and downs" with the host Algonquin nation but pointed to successful relationship-building initiatives.

She said the university has issued a tuition waiver for Algonquin students, with the Algonquin presence surging from 11 students to 53 students on campus since then. The university had a combined graduate and undergraduate enrolment of 12,300 in fall 2025.

"I feel that we have a responsibility given where we are situated and located, including being on the unceded traditional territory of the Algonquin nation to listen and and respond to the needs of that community," she said.

items: Agreement with Oblates hailed as major step in shining light on 'shameful history' of residential schools

blocks.text: As for the investigation into uOttawa's residential school connection, Sylvestre said the work is well underway with the university funding two researchers to comb the Oblates' archives.
"I'm certainly not proud of what we'll find, but I'm proud that we are doing this," she said.
"I think people say there's no reconciliation without truth, and I think it starts there."
There is also collective bargaining ongoing with the professors union where both parties are committing to supporting career progression for Indigenous faculty and resolving grievances more swiftly.

She said she intends to appoint a new associate vice-president, Indigenous engagement, while the university has already adopted an Indigenous verification policy. Strategies for better recruitment and retention of faculty members are in the works, she added.

articles.title: Why historic wins for women in Ontario's municipal elections are just 'half the battle'
articles.summary: Monday's municipal elections ushered in some notable wins for women across Ontario — with voters electing their first female mayors in some cities, new female mayors in several others and an…

image.caption: Voters head to the polls at St. Lawrence Market to cast a ballot in Toronto’s municipal and mayoral elections on Oct. 26, 2026. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Monday's municipal elections ushered in some notable wins for women across Ontario — with voters electing their first female mayors in some cities, new female mayors in several others, and an all-female council in a village southwest of Ottawa.

Official election results are still being calculated, but overall these are some encouraging signs that women are making inroads in Ontario municipal politics, said Tracey Raney, a professor in the department of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University.
"It’s great to see more women break through several glass ceilings in local governments across the province," Raney told CBC News.

Niagara Falls made history with its first female mayor, with Coun. Lori Lococo unseating the previous mayor, whom many considered unbeatable. Port Colborne also made history by electing Bea Kenny, who said she was "humbled" by her win, as its first female mayor.

North Bay, too, elected its first female mayor, and also has a female deputy mayor, putting women in complete control of the city's top leadership posts for the first time since it elected its first mayor in 1891.
"It's overdue, but I'm happy to be here and I can't wait to see what happens next," mayor-elect Maggie Horsfield said to reporters Monday.
‘I’m pretty excited about this’: Ottawa’s next council to have more women than men
Meanwhile, Ottawa's city council now has more women than men for the first time. Voters in the eastern Ontario municipality of Merrickville-Wolford just elected an all-female council.

And several jurisdictions have newly elected — although not their first — female mayors, including Kingston, Cornwall and Thunder Bay. In Toronto, Olivia Chow was re-elected decisively with about 54 per cent of the vote, according to the results so far.

items: Big wins, shocking losses, and goodbye to a 46-year mayor: what to know about Ontario's 400+ elections
Flurry of new mayors elected in eastern Ontario, preliminary results show

blocks.text: But there were also some setbacks, with highly visible female incumbents like Mississauga's Carolyn Parrish and Hamilton's Andrea Horwath facing defeat, notes Elizabeth Goodyear-Grant, a political studies professor at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont.
We're inching closer to gender parity in Canadian politics, "but the pace of change is very slow and setbacks do occur," Goodyear-Grant told CBC News.
"At the municipal level, the overall numbers in Ontario seem sort of stalled ... despite the notable gains in some jurisdictions."
'A historic first'
In Merrickville-Wolford, a picturesque village about 75 kilometres southwest of Ottawa, Anne Barr was on the road collecting election signs Tuesday morning after a successful campaign.

Barr, a longtime councillor and now the mayor-elect, garnered nearly twice as many votes as incumbent Michael Cameron. Voters also elected councillors Margaret Gural, Mary-Catherine Fraser, Cindy Hanna and Gina Jelmini, each with strong leads.

With that, the village of just over 3,000 people became one of a handful in Ontario to ever elect an all-female council. In 2018, two municipalities in Ontario — Algonquin Highlands and Spanish — made history with theirs. Before that, in 1967, Tweed elected the first all-female council in the province.
Anne Barr, the mayor-elect of Merrickville-Wolford, Ont., is part of a newly elected all-female council for the municipality. (Anne Barr)
Barr says she understands why Merrickville-Wolford’s newly elected all-female slate of councillors is attracting attention.
"It's a historic first for our municipality," she told CBC News, adding she was looking forward to working with such an "exceptional team."

"What’s most important, however, is that our residents have elected five capable individuals who bring deep roots in the community, a broad range of skills and experience and a shared commitment to working hard."
In Niagara Falls on Monday, Lori Lococo downplayed her gender after she was elected the city's first female mayor.
"I always hope that people vote for people based on their experience and skills, not because of their gender," she said.
Lori Lococo speaks after winning Niagara Falls mayoral race
A bottleneck stage for growth

The wins for women are more striking when you consider they made up just 32 per cent of the candidates province-wide, according to data from the Association of Municipalities of Ontario. That's only up a percentage point from 2022, when 31 per cent of candidates were female, although it's a jump from 27 per cent in 2018.
This reveals a bottleneck for growth in women’s share of council and mayoral positions, says Queen's University's Goodyear-Grant.
"If women aren’t running in equal proportions as men, it’s difficult to anticipate rapid or significant growth in their seat share," she said.

items: 'I’m not going to let them silence me:' women political candidates push back against growing hate
Andrea Horwath gives tearful address as outgoing mayor, saying it's been 'an honour to serve' Hamilton

blocks.text: It also highlights some of the barriers that women face in politics, she said, including less access to donors and fundraising, gendered stereotypes about their qualifications, and harassment on the campaign trail.

Several female Hamilton municipal politicians recently spoke out about the abuse they've faced, for instance. Horwath told CBC last week that the harassment is driving women out of politics, and it made her "seriously consider" whether to run this election.

In Brampton, Coun. Rowena Santos recently told local media she's faced serious threats to her physical safety during her time in office, including people who "said that I deserve to be raped and killed."

That's why getting women elected is just "half the battle," said Raney, with Toronto Metropolitan University — we also need to consider what happens once they take office, she said. That includes looking at whether they are being heard, able to influence the policy process or facing disproportionate scrutiny and harassment.
"Representation matters, but so does the ability to not have to face harassment and violence once you have a seat at the decision-making table," Raney said.
"The public also has a responsibility to hold elected officials accountable without resorting to personal attacks, harassment or intimidation."
North Bay mayor-elect Maggie Horsfield speaks with reporters

articles.title: Queen of Canada documentary director wants you to know her followers are still out there
articles.summary: CBC News spoke with Queen of Canada director Cristian Gomes and journalist Mack Lamoureux about their new documentary, and why it focuses on Romana Didulo's past followers.

image.caption: Romana Didulo, holding a bullhorn, at a rally at Parliament Hill in Ottawa. She is the subject of a new Passionate Eye documentary. (Fathom Film Group)

blocks.text: Entertainment·INTERVIEW
CBC News spoke with Queen of Canada director Cristian Gomes and journalist Mack Lamoureux about their new documentary, and why it focuses on Romana Didulo's past followers.
Director Cristian Gomes, journalist Mack Lamoureux on why their new documentary focuses on Romana's followers
A little over a year ago, the RCMP raided a purple schoolhouse in Saskatchewan that had been taken over by a woman known as the "QAnon Queen of Canada."

It was the fallout of a movement years in the making: a group now widely referred to as a cult led by Romana Didulo — a self-described shapeshifting alien who passed her own "laws" in her self-described "Kingdom of Canada."
That group has largely disbanded, but its past members remain. They are the subjects of a new documentary, Queen of Canada, airing on CBC's The Passionate Eye on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Because while the documentary does focus on Didulo's actions, she does not feature as an interview subject. Instead, director Cristian Gomes centres on those past followers, who both grapple with what they went through but who — in some cases — continue to believe in what they were working toward.
CBC News speaks with Gomes and subject Mack Lamoureux, the first journalist to seriously investigate and report on Didulo, about why that is so important.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
New doc Queen of Canada takes on Romana Didulo story

You speak to a number of people who followed Romana. They have since left her, but — as is shown in the documentary — they haven't given up many of their distrustful beliefs around the media and government. Was it hard to get them to talk to you?

Cristian Gomes: It was difficult to find the voices, only because I'm not a part of the ecosystem that they thrive in. But once you join them, once you figure out how to find their voice and engage with them online — like in places like Telegram and other really private chats — it isn't really hard to get them to talk.

It was a big learning lesson for me, as well. People to whose beliefs, at one point, I responded like 'These views are kind of abhorrent. They're really damaging, and they leak into all facets of society, actually.' But at the same time, they're human too. They're just people who are really lost and they're being taken advantage of.
Mack, I'm curious whether your interpretation might fall in line with Cristian's. Do you see this as a wider case study, one that illustrates that widening division within society?

Mack Lamoureux: I like to consider Romana a harbinger. I consider her a glimpse into a possible future that we're not necessarily tied to, but if we don't course-correct we could end up in that way. The disconnect from reality and the damage that her followers had was so extreme — and in many ways scary — that I do think that it's something that we need to try and take steps to fix.

The future looks bleak for a lot of people. On top of that, you have algorithms which are pushing people down these rabbit holes. You have influencers and media organizations who are all too happy to run with conspiracies if it means that they're going to strengthen their bottom dollar.

All of this adds into a toxic cocktail that can lead people to joining and following people like Romana and completely ruining their lives. The worse life gets for people, the more people are going to find their ways into the arms of bad actors like Romana.
Cult leader Romana Didulo set up a base in a decommissioned school in Richmound, Sask., in 2023. (CBC News)

The moment that stands out to me is when one of your interview subjects says she once told her adult son if he got the COVID-19 vaccine, she would kill herself. Speaking with you now, it does seem like this could be framed as, 'She feels so isolated, so ignored, that's why she felt she needed to make that statement.' Was that what you were going for?

CG: What is fascinating in the film is that the people who are making these statements have been through the process of a radicalization: being a part of a group, and then being disgruntled within that group and leaving it. And they still hold their views. And I think that really speaks to how deeply, deeply pushed to the fringes these people are.
They really have been totally put outside of the systems of politics in this country, and any other way they could express themselves. They have no outlet.

The dynamic between the character you're speaking about and her son is really interesting because her son, although he doesn't agree with all of her views, he found out how to have a relationship with her. And that's a big part of why she was able to leave the group.
That happens a lot in high-control groups; having someone on the outside who's just there to listen to you without judgment is what helps a lot of people leave.

items: Crown stays charges against self-proclaimed ‘Queen of Canada’
Saskatchewan mayor stepping down now that 'Queen of Canada' cult is gone

blocks.text: Mack, you've reported on cults and terrorist groups for years. How does healing work in that situation? Is there a way to fix this from a societal standpoint?

ML: For a lot of people, healing isn't a linear path, it's kind of hopping back and forth through these different things. And for a lot of these people, they're just not going to come back from it. And I think we need to be relatively OK with it. I think it's more about getting those folks to be a bit more of a functioning member of society than it is about trying to force them to believe our collective reality that we have.

I don't think there is a 'fixing it,' because I think it's an integral flaw in our design. But I do think that there are ways of making it better, because the technology that we have is accelerating it. But I don't think there is a world where we all hold hands and everything's fine. I wish I was a utopian, but…

items: Fjord's Sebastian Stan, Cristian Mungiu on making a movie no one can agree on
Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'

blocks.text: From your experience speaking with this group, Cristian, how has your interpretation changed? Is there a way to fix this situation, or will those who feel this ignored and separated continue to feel that way?
CG: A big part of this is people feeling like they have no voice. That's how they get ostracized. We all experience what it was like in COVID. We all experienced the polarization of it.

Something we have to realize is that there's this large group of Canadians who are very disenfranchised, who have been for a long time. They don't believe in political systems. Some of them don't even believe they're a part of Canada. They think they're in another sovereign state — that's how far they feel isolated from us.
And so when we see that happening and if we can acknowledge that's happening, we have to reach out to those people. We have to bring them back into the fold. We have to have conversations with them.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canada facing carbon tariff threat from European Union: internal documents
articles.summary: Canada is facing a carbon tariff threat from the European Union within months as the economic bloc fully implements its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is working to bring Canada closer to the European Union. But a tariff set to begin next year on industrial goods is for now still expected to go ahead. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Canada is facing a carbon tariff threat from the European Union within months as the economic bloc fully implements its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
No exemptions for Canada despite adopting carbon pricing
Canada is facing a carbon tariff threat from the European Union within months as the economic bloc fully implements its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).

According to internal documents CBC News obtained through an access to information request, Canadian iron, steel and aluminum are not exempt from the carbon tariff even with Canada's national price on carbon and its decade-old trade deal with the European Union.
The memo from Global Affairs Canada signed on Dec. 10, 2025, describes the CBAM as a "border charge" or "effectively a 'carbon tariff.'"

With the Canada-EU Summit this week in Montreal, Ottawa's diplomats continue to seek an agreement with Brussels before Canadian exporters face additional compliance costs and a carbon charge that European importers will have to pay at the border in 2027.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that the summit marks the start of negotiations for Canada to become a closer strategic partner to the 27-member bloc.

items: Canada's new relationship with EU will be 'closer to membership' than ever, senior officials say

blocks.text: Global Affairs estimates $2.8 billion worth of goods annually are exposed to the carbon import levy — primarily on metals that are already impacted by U.S tariffs.
The internal note flags "risks" with the implementation of the carbon tariff "occurring as Canada seeks to diversify trade away from the U.S. and toward markets like the EU."

It adds Canada's exposure to the tariff "appears modest" overall but the "potential impacts vary considerably across provinces and territories" — hitting Newfoundland and Labrador and Quebec particularly hard.

items: READ the internal note CBC News obtained

blocks.text: The briefing note states that an annual average of $885 million worth of the Atlantic province's iron and steel exports — almost half — are exposed to the EU's incoming tariff.
In Quebec the value of aluminum, iron and steel exports that are exposed amounts to about $792 million annually.
Those figures are averages based on data between 2021 and 2024, meaning exposure could be higher as Canadian goods seek new buyers to avoid U.S. tariffs.
'Big change' to trade regime
Climate trade experts have been warning about the pending EU carbon charge for some time.
"It's a big deal conceptually," said Ross-Linden Fraser, an acting director at the Canadian Climate Institute. "This is a big change in the way that trade gets treated."

The EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism is being applied at a low level and will ramp up to fully in 2034. It's meant to encourage exporters to lower the planet-warming emissions created when producing their industrial goods.

But Canadian steel, aluminum, iron and cement exporters are already incurring costs for compliance, having to measure the emissions embedded in their exports and have those figures reviewed by an accredited verifier.
"That's a costly prospect," said Aaron Cosbey, an economist who researches carbon border adjustments at the International Institute for Sustainable Development.

The EU, however, is exempting countries like Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and soon the U.K. That's because their carbon pricing systems are linked or fall under Europe's carbon market, the EU Emissions Trading System.

items: Will the Alberta-Canada carbon pricing deal work?
What comes next after Canada-Alberta energy deal?

blocks.text: The briefing note obtained by CBC News explicitly states that an "exemption … is not currently possible" for Canada because our carbon price is not linked to Europe's.
"In 2025, the EU carbon price is approximately $134 per tonne, compared to $95 per tonne [in Canada]," according to the briefing note.
The Carney government's recent energy accord with Alberta weakened Canada's carbon price further.
Canadian diplomats and ministers are "focused on minimizing" the impact of the carbon tariff on Canadian exporters in their engagements with the European Commission, according to the documents.
Countries that have a carbon price will get credit for that, according to the internal note, but it's not clear how the EU will recognize Canada's.
Canada engages EU on carbon tariffs
Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin will be attending the Canada-EU Summit in Montreal.

Her office previously noted that Canada has been "advocating for recognition of Canada’s industrial carbon pricing systems and streamlined approaches that avoid unnecessary administrative burdens for Canadian exporters."
In an interview with CBC News on Oct. 22, Dabrusin did not say whether negotiators were making progress.

"My goal always is to make sure that we have an industrial carbon pricing system that's effective and that works for making sure that our industry is competitive and that we are supporting Canadian jobs," Dabrusin said.
European Union officials briefing reporters ahead of the summit said both countries are "committed to [tackling] climate change."
With Europe moving ahead with the carbon border adjustment mechanism, both sides are working to have "the same kind of baselines, the same kind of processes," the officials said.
It's unclear though what that looks like.
One producer sees an edge

The threat of carbon tariffs for exporters is growing. The internal note speaks of "CBAM proliferation," flagging several countries developing or assessing carbon border adjustment mechanisms, including the United Kingdom, Australia, Japan and Turkey.
Canada's major metals producers Rio Tinto and ArcelorMittal declined to comment. But one exporter sees an upside.

Canada Nickel is advancing a nickel project in Timmins, Ont. With its access to low-carbon electricity and plans to capture carbon and store it underground, the company says it is well positioned to export what the industry calls potentially zero-carbon steel to Europe.

items: Minister gives Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts

blocks.text: It hasn't calculated the final costs, including administrative compliance, on its balance sheet. But compared with other global exporters, it estimates it will be minimal.
"We're looking to ship millions of tonnes of steel per year eventually to Europe … but that'll translate into pennies per tonne over the long run," said Canada Nickel CEO Mark Selby.
Not every producer may see it that way.
By the time Europe's carbon tariff fully kicks in by 2034, Cosbey estimates Canadian steel could cost an additional $150 per tonne.
"That's more than 10 per cent of the price of a tonne of steel on the open market these days. So that's a significant cost," Cosbey said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

David Thurton is a senior reporter in CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. He covers daily politics in the nation’s capital and specializes in environment and energy policy. Born in Canada but raised in Trinidad and Tobago, he’s moved around more times than he can count. He’s worked for CBC in several provinces and territories, including Alberta and the Northwest Territories. He can be reached at david.thurton@cbc.ca

articles.title: Deaths associated with wildfire smoke up about 275% in Canada, new report says
articles.summary: Deaths linked to wildfire smoke in Canada have exploded by 275 per cent since the early 2000s according to a major global report that says the change is largely due to human-caused climate change.

image.caption: A woman bikes along the waterfront in Toronto as wildfire smoke fills the city, on July 15. Such smoke has been associated with approximately 4,000 deaths in Canada each year, between 2021-25, according to new research published Tuesday in the medical journal The Lancet. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian

blocks.text: Health
Deaths linked to wildfire smoke in Canada have exploded by 275 per cent since the early 2000s according to a major global report that says the change is largely due to human-caused climate change.
Scientists find that health impacts of climate change have escalated in last decade
Deaths linked to wildfire smoke in Canada have exploded by about 275 per cent since the early 2000s according to a major global report that tracks connections between health and climate change.

The report, published Tuesday in The Lancet, found that an average of approximately 4,000 deaths were associated with wildfire smoke in Canada each year between 2021-25. That's compared with an average of only 1,050 annually in 2003-12.

Ian Hamilton, the chair in planetary health at the George Institute for Global Health at Imperial College in London, co-authored the study, which comes a decade since the prestigious medical journal began tracking the health impacts of climate change.
He says it looked at how many additional people died during periods of wildfire smoke compared with historical records, rather than count case by case.
"For any individual, it might not be that [wildfire smoke] was the trigger," he said. "But on average across the population, we're seeing more death associated with those periods."

Hamilton says the year range used for wildfire smoke-associated deaths, 2003-12, is meant to represent a historical baseline. The scientists chose different sets of dates as the baselines of different phenomena.

According to the report, Canada lost approximately 5.2 million hectares of tree cover in 2024, 148 per cent more than in 2016 — and wildfires accounted for 86 per cent of the loss. That meant an increase in wildfire smoke, and the loss of natural cooling systems like shade that can provide some relief on Canada's hottest days.
How to protect yourself from wildfire smoke
Tragic consequences

The study looked at other heat-related risks. For example, it says the number of hours people in Canada were exposed to potentially dangerous heat during physical activity — for example, going on brisk walks on hot days –- increased by 36 hours annually in 2016-25, compared with during the 1990s.
Dr. Courtney Howard, chair of the Global Climate and Health Alliance and the president-elect of the Canadian Medical Association, says that shift can be particularly dangerous for young athletes.
"Young people are almost so strong, especially athletes, that they push through heat and heat related exhaustion," she said. "And unfortunately that can actually lead to mortality."
Howard says that the reality of climate change is steadily getting worse.
"We're not at a new normal," she said. "There's no flat line currently on the emissions graph, and therefore there is no flat line in terms of the heat."
A man cools off at a temporary misting station in Vancouver during a heat wave that gripped the city in August 2023. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

Dr. Anna Gunz, a pediatrician in London, Ont., says that she's seen the consequences of heat-related illness first hand, recalling a young patient who went into cardiac arrest while playing outside and then died. When tests showed the patient's asthma had been the cause, Gunz says his mother's immediate response was "Oh, it was really humid out today."
"It sends chills down my spine," Gunz said, to hear a parent relate their child's death to the weather.
LISTEN | More than a nuisance:
Front Burner28:11The true toll of wildfire smoke
Not just an exercise
The report also says 80 per cent of Canada's heatwave days in 2025 were directly attributable to fossil fuel-driven climate change.
Hamilton says the numbers are not just a modelling exercise.
It looks back and asks, "Under the same conditions, what were we experiencing 10, 15, 25, 50 years ago?" he said. "And what are we experiencing now?"
The difference, he says, is that we have a lot more carbon dioxide in our atmosphere.

items: Canadians should prepare for a 5 C hotter future, report warns
Wildfires are reversing Canada's progress on improving air quality

blocks.text: Howard says Canada needs to invest in adapting to the changing climate, pointing to the growing need for air conditioning in many regions, and the need to upgrade health facilities to cope with wildfire smoke.
"We need to know that this is going to keep getting worse year on year and year, unless we decrease greenhouse gas emissions," she said.
"Decreasing greenhouse gas emissions is the most important adaptation."
Why distance doesn’t make wildfire smoke safer
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kiera Osborne is a journalist based out of Toronto. She previously interned with the Health, Science and Climate Change content units at CBC and holds a bachelor of medical sciences from Western University.

articles.title: Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections
articles.summary: While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend. A…

image.caption: Supporters of Bobby Pulido, the Democratic Party candidate for the U.S. House of Representatives in a South Texas district, stationed outside a polling station in Edinburg, Texas, during early voting for the U.S. midterm elections. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New

While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend. A willingness to cast ballots across party lines has made the roughly 39 million Hispanic eligible voters a crucial demographic at election time, courted equally by Democrats and Republicans.
Hispanic voters have soured on Republicans over ICE and economy — but many don't vote along party lines
While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend.

A willingness to cast ballots across party lines has made the roughly 39 million Hispanic eligible voters in the U.S. a crucial demographic at election time, courted equally by Democrats and Republicans.
They swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024.

But if their current dissatisfaction with Trump's performance as president translates into votes in next Tuesday's midterms, the Latino community could potentially sway some crucial races and tip the balance of power in Congress toward the Democrats.

Latinos are the "swingiest" voters in the nation, says Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, which advocates for the 4.5 million Hispanic-owned companies (small and large) across the country.

"We are a community that doesn't vote party, it votes person," Palomarez told CBC News. "You'll see Republicans willing to vote for a Democrat in the Hispanic community very often, and conversely Democrats willing to go for a Republican."

U.S. President Donald Trump travelled to Corpus Christi, Texas, for a campaign rally on Tuesday to try to boost support for Republican midterm candidates in the largely Hispanic districts of south Texas. (Eric Vryn/The Associated Press)
Trump increased his share of Hispanic voters in each successive election since 2016, garnering the highest percentage ever for a Republican presidential candidate in 2024, according to exit polls.
Yet the very issues that drove Hispanic support for Trump in 2024 — reducing the cost of living and tightening border security — could be the ones that hurt the Republicans in the 2026 midterms.
ICE tactics draw fire
Some Hispanic voters are focused on how Trump's decision to go to war with Iran triggered a sharp rise in the price of gas and diesel across the U.S.

Others are deeply concerned by the way Trump dramatically ramped up detention of undocumented Hispanics who've lived upstanding lives in the U.S. for years, rather than sticking to his pledge of deporting violent criminals.

items: How Canada and tariffs are factoring into U.S. midterm elections

blocks.text: In Texas, where Hispanics make up roughly one-third of eligible voters, disenchantment with Trump and the Republicans is palpable in the Latino-majority cities of the Rio Grande Valley.

CBC News shadowed a team of get-out-the-vote canvassers for LUPE Votes — an activist group whose name, La Unión del Pueblo Entero, translates as "union of all the people" — in the border city of Edinburg.

Canvassers with the activist group LUPE Votes prepare to knock on doors in the predominantly Hispanic city of Edinburg, Texas, with early voting under way in the U.S. midterms. José Ferrer, right, says his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and later deported. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

One of the canvassers, 24-year-old Jose Ferrer, said his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Father's Day this year. The family found his truck abandoned at the side of the road and didn't hear from him for two weeks. He was deported to Mexico two months later.

"I'm not the only one getting affected, obviously," Ferrer told CBC News. His mother-in-law, a teacher, has described her students' parents being grabbed by ICE agents while waiting for the school bus.
ICE enforcement 'brutal' in south Texas: developer
The anger in the community over ICE tactics cuts across economic lines.

Mario Guerrero, a developer who voted for Trump three times because he considered him a very successful businessman, says immigration enforcement is one of the key reasons he'll vote Democrat on the midterm ballot.
"I believe in the American dream," Guerrero said in an interview at the site of a supermarket he's building beside a new housing development in Pharr, next door to Edinburg.

"The ICE enforcement that we've been seeing here in south Texas has been brutal," he said, adding that the job-site and roadside raids have scared off so many people from coming to work that the pace of construction projects slowed to a crawl.
Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, oversees work on a grocery store his company is building on the edge of a residential subdivision in Pharr, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"All of our workers are documented," Guerrero said. "The problem is [ICE agents are] apprehending, they're taking people with the proper documentation."
He believes the tactics will have midterm consequences for the Republicans, including "a turnout of Mexican Americans like they've never seen before."
Hispanic voting bloc defies generalization
Hispanic people now account for one-sixth of the eligible voters in the U.S., a larger group than Black Americans, according to data compiled by Pew Research Center.

But they defy broad generalizations as a voting bloc. They encompass devout Catholics, fiscally conservative entrepreneurs, working class immigrants-turned-citizens and college-educated Hispanics whose families have been in the U.S. for generations.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency

blocks.text: "We have seen over and over with data that we cannot put Latino voters in one category," said Dayana Iza, Texas director of Mi Familia Vota, a national organization that aims to build Latino political power.
She describes the group's work as helping Hispanic Americans "connect the dots" to understand how elections can have a tangible impact on their daily lives.
Álvaro Corral, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, specializes in the politics of Latino voters in the U.S. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
"That is what is really going to make a difference with how Latinos turn out for these midterms," Iza told CBC News.
"There are a lot of Latinos that still do not participate in this electoral process, and those are the folks that we're really trying to target."
Nuance on immigration, border security
But even if there is a notable shift away from the Republicans at the midterms, it won't necessarily mean that Hispanic voters are fully embracing everything about the Democratic Party.

Neither party has accurately reflected the nuanced position of the typical Hispanic voter on immigration and border security, says Álvaro Corral, political science professor at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.
He says that position combines strong measures to keep criminals from flowing across the border with a pathway to citizenship for undocumented migrants who've long worked in the U.S.
Instead, the Trump administration's approach "is really offending the sensibilities and morality of a large portion of the Latino voters," Corral told CBC News.
Palomarez, of the U.S Hispanic Business Council, says the Democrats "took the Hispanic vote for granted" and at the national level shifted "a bit too left for the Hispanic community's liking."
That leeriness about the Democrats can be seen in the campaigns of some of their own Hispanic candidates.
Bobby Pulido, left, campaigning recently at a seniors' activity center in McAllen, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)
'Not Team Red. Not Team Blue'

Bobby Pulido, the Latino recording star who's trying to unseat incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz in the 15th congressional district of Texas, downplays his party in his campaign ads and material.
"Not Team Red. Not Team Blue. Team You," says a slogan on the T-shirts worn by Pulido's campaign workers.

items: How high inflation is hurting Trump's Republicans in U.S. midterm campaign
Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump

blocks.text: "Hispanics, they're not so partisan. It's very much, 'Are you gonna go fight for me?' That's what matters," Pulido told CBC News in an interview after he campaigned at a seniors' activity centre.
Still, Pulido says Hispanic Americans will punish Republican candidates in the midterms because they hate how ICE raids both separate families and disrupt the economy.
"When you add those two things, it's a very, very big explosion and you're going to see this Nov. 3."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

articles.title: Democrats promise Epstein probes will be a priority if they win midterms, but to what end?
articles.summary: Democrats have hammered Republican opponents and Donald Trump's administration with midterm ads featuring a man dead for seven years, Jeffrey Epstein. Despite being a part of congressional efforts…

image.caption: Donald Trump, left, with the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, centre, in a photo released by Democrats on the House's oversight committee on Dec. 12, 2025. It was later reported that the picture was from a 1997 event in New York City, with Belgian model Ingrid Seynhaeve als

blocks.text: Pro and college football fans in the U.S. were just treated to another fall weekend of thrilling finishes, controversial calls and, during commercial breaks, nearly wall-to-wall midterm campaign ads.

The games are some of the highest-rated programs left on linear television, and much of the messaging from Democratic candidates highlighted what are said to be failings of the Donald Trump administration's handling of the release and investigation of the Jeffrey Epstein files.

Democrats have spent $53 million US on ads mentioning the late sex offender in competitive races, compared to $3 million from Republicans, the Washington Post recently reported, citing figures from political spending trackers AdImpact. During the 2024 presidential campaign, according to CNN, Epstein featured in just three campaign ads, all involving candidates in Florida, where he kept his main residence.

If Democrats regain control of one or both houses of Congress after the Nov. 3 vote, learning more about Epstein will be "one of our top priorities," according to a recent interview Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who sits on the House's oversight committee, had with Bloomberg News.
Two pieces of legislation already introduced in Congress could be among the avenues they pursue.

But former federal prosecutor Ankush Khardori has suggested Democrats, if they prevail, should instead focus on the abundant examples of potential corruption by Donald Trump's administration and family members over the past two years.

Khardori has called the release of contextless Epstein documents beginning last year "a historic mistake" which has led to censorious, but uneven, consequences for those who merely knew the man but have never been accused of a crime.

Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia of California, shown on Capitol Hill on Sept. 22, has indicated that if his party wins control of the House or Senate in the midterms that investigating matters related to Epstein's abuse will continue. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

"The presumption of innocence has been turned on its head. We have countenanced an ethos of guilt by association," he wrote in a Boston Globe op-ed, reproduced on his website. Khardori draws attention to the April suicide of Norway's Edward Juul Rod-Larsen, whose family, and mostly his parents, faced questions about their contacts with Epstein.

Nearly one year after the enactment of the Epstein Files Transparency Act and over 19 interviews done by the House's oversight committee, "a key claim made by lawmakers and other advocates for disclosure — that the Justice Department’s files would expose a hidden child sex trafficking ring — has not been substantiated," he wrote.
Khardori says Democrats could assign a respected prosecutor to oversee an Epstein-related commission if they truly feel there's more to learn.
2 criminal referrals made

Providing more evidence than what previously existed was always going to prove a formidable task, given Epstein's death and accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell's questionable credibility given she's serving a lengthy prison sentence. Add to that the fact that three of the many women who said they were abused by Epstein are no longer alive, nor are a handful of the many notable people, mostly men, who spent time with Epstein.
Did Jeffrey Epstein really introduce Donald Trump and Melania?

Rep. James Comer, the Kentucky Republican who has been leading the House oversight committee, made two referrals to the Justice Department earlier this year based on testimony from Sarah Kellen, a former Epstein assistant. She accused two men of sexual assault in separate encounters, while making clear that neither Epstein nor Maxwell helped facilitate the alleged abuse.

The Justice Department does not comment on ongoing probes, and is not required to act upon a congressional referral, so it's not clear if they're pursuing those leads. But the difficulties of establishing guilt in sexual assault allegations that are many years old have been demonstrated in cases involving powerful and well-defended men like Peter Nygard, Frank Stronach and Harvey Weinstein, cases where some charges have been dropped and retrials have occurred.

And were a case ever to reach trial, Kellen would likely be asked about problematic allegations levelled by some women that Kellen, an adult at the time she knew Epstein and Maxwell, helped facilitate abuse.
Lawmakers want access

Democrat Ro Khanna and Republican Thomas Massie, who led the charge in the House in getting the Transparency Act passed, are among five co-sponsors of a follow-up bill to address what they say are failings of the Justice Department. The proposed legislation could open the door for state attorneys general and survivors to sue the department for access to unredacted files that have currently been held back by the administration, which claims they are too sensitive or privileged, as in the case of lawyer-client communications, to release.

Garcia and Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren have also hinted at what else could come by recently introducing the Epstein Wall Street Records Act, which would require regulators "to disclose supervisory records related to Epstein and his associates" and to "investigate Epstein-connected banks and executives for possible banking, securities, or illicit financing violations."
House members Ro Khanna of California, left, and Thomas Massie, centre, are shown with survivors who spoke about Epstein on Nov. 18, 2025. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)
Democrats have accused at least three major financial institutions of not properly following anti-money laundering laws to report large, suspicious transactions with Epstein's accounts.

Garcia, per the Bloomberg report, also seemed to suggest that bringing back some witnesses for another appearance, but under oath, could prove more fruitful. Those who've appeared for interviews, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, were advised before questioning that they had an obligation to tell the truth.

But if witnesses are brought back, lawmakers might want to hold more focused sessions. CBC News has read all publicly available transcripts from the oversight committee and the sessions were often repetitive — legislators dipped in and out due to their other duties, often asking questions already posed by colleagues.
LISTEN | Evidence of Epstein's relationships:
Front Burner31:06Epstein’s orbit: will justice come?

Several lines of inquiry seemed to offer debatable value — multiple witnesses who visited Epstein's New York townhouse were asked about the strange painting of Clinton in a blue dress that the financier possessed, while many others, regardless of their occupation or connection to Epstein, were asked point blank if they could offer any information supporting the idea that he was working for Mossad or some other foreign intelligence service.

Nearly every witness was read a list of mostly famous names known to have spent time with Epstein — from Woody Allen to Noam Chomsky to Ehud Barak — to see if they, too, had interactions with those individuals, calling to mind Hillary Clinton's comment after her interview that the panel was on a "fishing expedition."

Trump has described Epstein as an acquaintance, though others have said their relationship, at least in the 1990s, was more friendly. While the explanations for why Trump broke off communications have differed, it appears he was no longer in contact with Epstein for some time when the financier was indicted in Florida in 2006.

As if to remind voters of sexual misconduct allegations Trump himself has faced in the past, whether they watch football or not, Democrats on Monday followed up the campaign ads with a report from their judiciary committee members that collects seemingly every damning mention of Trump in the Epstein file dump so far, including allegations of sexual abuse and rape.

items: What we learned from Bill Gates's interview with Congress about Epstein
6 takeaways from Bill Clinton's deposition about Epstein and Maxwell

blocks.text: At least one allegation was publicly reported as far back as the 2016 presidential election, while another one other emerged during the 2024 campaign in a more limited form. Now, that same accuser alleges she wasn't just groped by Trump in an alleged 1993 incident, but raped.
The most shocking information concerns alleged incidents with a young teen, even though a civil suit related to that case was twice dropped by the anonymous plaintiff's lawyers over a decade ago.
Trump has never been formally accused of a crime with respect to activities related to his Epstein friendship.

The House Democrats recommended a special counsel be appointed to investigate the allegations, something only the attorney general can do. In a week's time, however, the Democrats could have more levers to get to damaging information they appear to sincerely believe they can find.

items: House committee asks U.S. DOJ to examine sexual abuse allegations made by ex-Epstein assistant

articles.title: Smaller airlines ask Transport Canada for pilots' shifts to last up to 14 hours
articles.summary: At least 18 carriers are asking the federal government to extend their pilots' maximum flight duty period by an hour a day, saying the current rules prevent them from managing the frequent delays…

image.caption: An Air Inuit aircraft lands Kuujjuaq, in northern Quebec. The carrier is one of at least 18 that have requested an exemption from regulations regarding pilot flight times. (Félix Lebel/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: At least 18 carriers are asking the federal government to extend their pilots' maximum flight duty period by an hour a day, saying the current rules prevent them from managing the frequent delays that disrupt air travel in the North.
Their request faces staunch opposition from the country's main pilot union, which says it could lead to further exemptions and push pilot fatigue to dangerous levels.

The maximum daily flight duty period — the time from arrival at work until the last engine shutdown — would go from 13 to 14 hours, while the weekly limit would climb from 60 to 70 hours, according to exemption requests filed earlier this year with Transport Canada.
Overall, pilots could work up to 210 hours over a 28-day period, instead of the 192 hours currently allowed.
The view from inside the cockpit of an Air Inuit B-737 in northern Quebec. (Jonah Schantz/Air Inuit)

The airlines are primarily active in the most remote regions of the country. They say the regulations governing air travel since 2020 aren't suited for the unpredictable weather and underfunded airport facilities in the North.
They are seeking the changes to be part of draft regulations underway by Transport Canada to provide greater flexibility to air carriers.
"It was a one-size-fits-all for everyone, and that can't be the way it works," said Bernard Gervais, executive director of the Northern Air Transportation Association.
"What we're asking is for the rules to be applied according to the size of the operator and the operations they carry out."
Sleep experts say a high level of fatigue is comparable to a state of impairment from alcohol, which is especially concerning when it comes to piloting a plane.
Symptoms include short-term memory lapses, slower reaction times and reduced ability to prioritize tasks or assess risk.
The maximum number of work hours that can still be considered safe is at the heart of the debate between carriers and pilots.
Tim Perry is president of ALPA Canada, the country's major pilots' union. He says longer pilot hours come with serious risks. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
"You need to hear us when we say what's being contemplated is potentially very unsafe," said Tim Perry, president of ALPA Canada, a union that represents more than 10,000 pilots in the country.
"This seems to us in our professional assessment to be about profits."

The Canadian regulations are complicated and vary according to several criteria, including departure and arrival times, the number of segments being flown and the number of days off that are spent at home.
A fatigue risk-management system already exists to allow carriers some flexibility, but the process is complex and costly, especially for smaller air carriers.
ALPA Canada represents pilots at some of the carriers making the exemption requests, but other regional operations are non-unionized.

"If one carrier gets an exemption, it will be seen as a competitive advantage," Perry said. "It would pave the way for further exemptions to be issued, and it would be difficult to know where to draw the line."
The National Airlines Council of Canada, which represents several major carriers (Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Jazz), declined to comment on the proposed changes.

items: Incoming Air Canada CEO's current airline engaged in 'anti-labour' behaviour, says Canadian union head

blocks.text: When Canada adopted stricter measures in 2020 to regulate pilots' schedules and bring the country’s rules in line with international standards, many carriers criticized them from the onset.
They argued the rules forced them to hire more pilots and hindered their ability to adapt to unpredictable circumstances such as fog, flat tires or runway closures.
"In the case of remote communities, if those interruptions turn into flight cancellations rather than delays, there is a real impact," said Joe Sparling, president of Yukon-based Air North.
"If you have a medical travel passenger that's going south for an appointment and the plane doesn't get in and misses by a day, then their appointment has to be rescheduled."

A mechanic walks up to a Nolinor Aviation aircraft in Mirabel, Que., last year. The airline says the realities of flying in the North require different regulations. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
Nolinor, which specializes in charter flights, says it needs to station pilots in Val d'Or, Que., just in case delays up north prevent the regular crew from flying back south.
"The regulations weren't designed to reflect the realities of the Arctic," said Nolinor's vice-president of operations, Yves Bergeron. "The reality in Montreal is not the same as in Iqaluit."
According to several people involved in the matter, Transport Canada's draft regulations have been stalled — and what comes next depends on federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon.

items: Canadians might be soon waiting longer to have their air travel complaints heard

blocks.text: "It's very political. The minister will decide," said Gervais from the industry association of northern carriers.
The pilots' union wants the minister to block the requested changes to maximum flight duty hours.
MacKinnon's office said officials at Transport Canada are still working on the file.

"The safety of civil aviation operations remains the department's top priority, and it is committed to maintaining rigorous and effective oversight of the entire system," said spokesperson Philippe-Alexandre Langlois.
Fatigue already a risk: experts

Matthew van Wollen, a Canadian fatigue specialist who works at Pulsar Informatics in the United States, says there are ways to safely lengthen Canadian pilots' shifts with "simpler and more unique operating profiles."
He has worked with Transport Canada and several Canadian carriers, but says his comments are based on scientific evidence.
He laid out three factors that influence a state of fatigue: whether the work period extends into the middle of the night, overall shift length and any accumulated sleep deficit.
Could the jet fuel crisis change your travel plans?
Van Wollen said many pilots might be happy to work longer hours over a number of days, in order to then benefit from more days off.
He said the priority for carriers should be managing the risk of fatigue on a daily basis.
"Just because you're following the rules doesn't mean you're safe. It doesn't mean you have no fatigue," he said.
Another expert in the field of sleep, Clinton Marquardt, said it would be helpful to set parameters for each carrier in collaboration with their pilots.
"That's the only way it's going to be solved in a satisfactory fashion," said Marquardt, a former official at the Transportation Safety Board.
While he said "operational needs and workforce desires" can't be ignored, they are not "the foundation of the system."
He said scientific evidence must be used to determine the proper rules.
Airlines say their pilots can always cancel a flight if they are too tired. They also say they are willing to monitor the impact of any changes to pilot schedules and make adjustments as needed.
"We're not aiming to plan 14-hour days every day," said Jonathan Lukca, a manager in charge of operations at Air Inuit.
"When the limit is reached, safety can be compromised and pilots might quit and go elsewhere. That's not in anyone's interest."

articles.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
articles.summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".

blocks.text: A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.
The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".
It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (£6,000) from $1,800.

The company said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.
The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for scam centres.
The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.
Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.
The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.
"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," one passenger, Holly Hennessey, told the BBC from Cambodia.
"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."
The Villa Vie Odyssey is equipped with several bars and restaurants, a pool deck and a pickleball court, according to its website.
Permanent residencies in its cabins range from $120,000 to $440,000. These cabins are also also available for rent from $3,500 a month.
Last year, the company launched a lifetime residence programme for people to spend their retirement years at sea.

In 2024, days after US President Donald Trump won his second term, Villa Vie Residences announced a four-year "Skip Forward" package. Its CEO told Fox Business at the time that it was the "perfect product for those who said they'd leave the country if 'XYZ' wins the election".

Hennessey said the ship's residents had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed". Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.
But some, like Hennessey, have decided to stick around in Cambodia in the hopes that the Villa Vie Odyssey will set sail again soon.
"Until they say we are done - done done - I am not giving up. I could never duplicate this lifestyle. The idea of going home? It would be so trite," she said.
"Cambodia's not the worst place to hang out."

items: Manuel V. Pangilinan is rebranding SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) to MGEN Renewables Inc. (MGENR) and integrating nearly P5 billion worth of renewable energy businesses.

The rebranding is part of a broader strategy by the Meralco group, distancing from the controversial past of Leandro Leviste's Solar Philippines, which faced contract terminations and financial obligations.
MGEN Renewables plans to strengthen its position by acquiring stakes in five solar businesses and is considering a 're-IPO' in March 2027, with expectations of improved financial performance.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Manuel V. Pangilinan is giving Leandro Leviste’s old solar crown jewel quite the makeover. First, shed the SPNEC name. Next, bring in nearly P5 billion worth of other renewable energy businesses.
And perhaps, pitch the shiny new thing to stock market investors all over again.

SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) is now officially MGEN Renewables Inc., (MGENR) after securing Securities and Exchange Commission approval on Monday, October 26; its stock ticker is also set to change to MGENR.

Officially, the renaming is part of the Meralco group’s broader rebranding strategy. Conveniently, it also removes a reminder of Solar Philippines, the controversial empire Leviste built before Pangilinan’s group took control.
And there’s quite a history behind SPNEC.

blocks.caption: FROM SPNEC to MGENR. This Rappler diagram shows the ownership of the rebranded solar company as of September 1, 2026 and before the proposed share swap. Diagram by Raphael Reyes/Rappler.

blocks.text: Leviste made his fortune assembling landholdings and securing solar development rights that attracted deep-pocketed investors, including Pangilinan himself. Industry sources that Rappler spoke with describe the young billionaire as a talented “flipper.”
But getting the rights to build solar farms and actually getting them built are two different businesses.

The Department of Energy (DOE) terminated 33 contracts tied to Leviste’s wider Solar Philippines group, covering around 11,400 megawatts of proposed capacity, and sought around P24 billion in financial obligations. His camp disputes the claims.
While much of the P24-billion mess relates to Leviste’s other companies, SPNEC is dragged into this too.
In a December 23, 2025 letter seen by Rappler, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin terminated the service contract for SPNEC’s 280-megawatt Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 project and demanded P10.34 billion.

The DOE cited missed work-program commitments, an unrenewed performance bond, and missing documents, including a feasibility study and proof of land rights. Most of the demand came from P12.38 billion in work-program commitments, less P2.04 billion credited for reported accomplishments.

MGEN insists SPNEC is legally separate from Solar Philippines and not liable for the wider group’s P24 billion obligation. But it acknowledges that Santa Rosa belongs to SPNEC and says that it invoked force majeure over transmission delays and sought reconsideration.
Separately, Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, face graft and plunder complaints involving solar contracts awarded to Leviste-linked companies. Both deny wrongdoing.

Leviste himself has kept his distance from his now Meralco-controlled company, resigning from the board in January and cashing out P3-billion worth of shares, leaving his holding company with an 11.51% stake.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] As Leandro Leviste cashes out of SPNEC, his private companies remain at the table

blocks.text: So, what’s next for MGENR?

On Tuesday, October 27, MGEN Renewables’ board approved a proposed P4.98-billion deal to take in stakes in five solar businesses from its controlling shareholder, MGEN Renewable Energy Inc., another Meralco subsidiary.
The companies have interests in operating solar plants across Luzon:

items: Greenergy for Global Inc. – 52.7-megawatt solar plant in Isabela
Greentech Solar Energy Inc. – 19.8-megawatt solar plant in Nueva Ecija
CACI Power Corporation – Linked to an 80.1-megawatt solar plant in Rizal
Nuevo Solar Energy Corporation – 68.7-megawatt solar plant in Ilocos Norte
PowerSource First Bulacan Solar Inc. – 55-megawatt solar plant in Bulacan

blocks.text: Instead of paying cash, MGEN Renewables will issue around 3.1 billion new shares to its controlling shareholder. If completed, the share swap deal would strengthen Meralco’s control while further diluting Leviste and other investors.
Then comes the more intriguing possibility, a “re-IPO” targeted for March 2027.
Since Leviste already took SPNEC public in 2021, this would be another share offering in the now bigger company under Meralco’s control, rather than a second listing. Nothing has been finalized.

This time, there’s more to show investors. Its P200-billion MTerra Solar project began commercial operations in August, while MGEN Renewables forecasts P774 million in profit for 2026, reversing a P4.1-billion loss in 2025.
The group also plans to invest up to another P7.815 billion in Terra Solar, subject to lender and investor approvals. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Marcos: Don't panic over peso fall to P64 per dollar
articles.summary: President Marcos Jr. says rising oil prices are weighing on the currency and economy.

blocks.text: October 28, 2026 | 3:32pm
MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. urged the public not to panic after the peso weakened to P64 against the dollar for the first time.
"Don't panic. It is an effect of still the rising prices of oil and subsequently the rising prices of fuel and its effect on the economy," Marcos said Wednesday, October 28.
He said the government's policy is to defend the peso as much as possible.

"People can take solace to the fact that our policy towards the peso is to continue to defend the peso as hard as possibly we can. We have all the tools to defend the peso. We have all the means to defend the peso," Marcos said.
The President also said the government was doing everything it could to bring down food prices.

The currency has been under sustained pressure in recent weeks, repeatedly hitting record lows against the dollar. On Monday alone, it closed at P63.95, marking the fifth straight trading day of decline and the 32nd record-low close this year. — Reports from Geraldine Santos

articles.title: Palace: P50-million bounty on Bato dela Rosa shows use of confidential funds
articles.summary: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro justified the interior department's P50 million bounty on at-large Sen. Bato dela Rosa, saying confidential funds should be used on such operations.

blocks.text: October 28, 2026 | 3:23pm

DILG Secretary Jonvic Remulla and PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. hold a press briefing at Camp Crame to announce a P50- million reward for the arrest of Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, whom they consider ‘armed and dangerous.’
The Philippine STAR / Miguel De Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Palace on Tuesday, October 27, again defended the P50-million bounty for information that will lead to the arrest of Sen. Ronald "Bato" dela Rosa, clarifying that the money will come from the interior department's intelligence and confidential funds, not from the president.

"Ito ang mga operasyon na dapat na pinaglalaanan talaga ng pondo. Pero kung ito ay istratehiya nila, para mas mapabilis ang paghuli kay Sen. Bato, hindi ibig sabihin na dapat pang manggaling kay Pangulo na magsabi na 'ito ang dapat ninyong ibigay na bounty’ dahil ang DILG (Department of Interior and Local Government) at PNP (Philippine National Police) ay mayroong sariling mandato at mayroon po silang sariling pondo," she said.

(These are the operations that should be funded. But if this is their strategy to speed up Sen. Bato's capture, the president does not need to dictate the size of the bounty because the DILG and PNP have their own mandates and funding.)
The bounty was announced on October 23 during a press briefing by Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, where Dela Rosa was declared "armed and dangerous."
Remulla also gave Dela Rosa a week-long deadline to surrender, which will lapse on Thursday, October 29.
According to Castro, the deadline was given to allow the fugitive senator to surrender "properly and without needing police intervention."
"But if a person asked to surrender is stubborn and seems to be taking advantage of the government and law enforcement, they will be hunted down," she added.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant of arrest for Dela Rosa in November 2025 in connection with charges of crimes against humanity linked to the Duterte administration’s war on drugs. Dela Rosa, now the most wanted fugitive in the country, led the national police force during the initial and most intensive phase of the anti-drug crackdown.

Former president Rodrigo Duterte was charged with crimes against humanity of murder and is currently detained at the ICC Detention Center at The Hague in the Netherlands. The opening of Duterte's trial is scheduled for Nov. 30, 2026.
