articles.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
articles.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.

blocks.text: Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week, external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.
The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.
The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.
China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children.
The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.
At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.
"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.
China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy, which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.
The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.
But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.
Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.
Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.
The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.
Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.
It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

articles.title: Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
articles.summary: Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained and fined over licensing violations. Rights groups condemned the ruling as a major blow to press freedom in Egypt, where independent media face…

image.caption: Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained after an Egyptian court ordered the closure of her news outlet [FILE: December 28, 2020]Image: Khaled Desouki/AFP

blocks.text: An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a license.
Attalah, one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine.
The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated.

Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country.
What happened during Lina Attalah's trial?
Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo.

According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP.
The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah.
She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order.
During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds.
That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11.
Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr?
Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017.
The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022.
Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.
Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind.
Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation.
How have press freedom groups reacted?
The ruling drew widespread international condemnation.

A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."
"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said.
Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful."
"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah.
US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime."
What is the state of press freedom in Egypt?
The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism.
Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses.
Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests.
The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations.
On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years.
According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work.

articles.title: Trump shows off tanker with ‘1m barrels of oil’ and floats Venezuela as 51st state
articles.summary:
President at Texas campaign rally hails deal struck with post-Maduro government as ‘greatest oil victory in history’

Donald Trump suggested Venezuela become the 51st state of the United…

blocks.text: Donald Trump suggested Venezuela become the 51st state of the United States on Tuesday as the president showed off a tanker he claimed had “one million barrels of oil on it” from the country, nine months after deposing its president.
At a campaign rally in Corpus Christ, Texas, Trump touted a US oil deal with Venezuela, which the US attacked in January, capturing its long-serving leader Nicolás Maduro.
Trump claims the agreement – struck with the South American country’s interim government, which is backed by Trump’s administration – will cover “billions” of barrels of oil.
Venezuela “will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe some day soon it’ll become a prosperous 51st state,” Trump said at the podium on Tuesday. “That’s possible.”
Venezuela is on a growing list of countries and territories Trump has spoken of acquiring, including Greenland, Canada and Mexico.

With tens of millions of Americans set to vote in next week’s midterm elections, Trump’s aggressive foreign policy – including his controversial war on Iran, and tariffs on goods from much of the world – have challenged his popularity, according to opinion polls, with his approval ratings falling to record lows.

But on Tuesday, the president sought to point to the Venezuela operation as an example of his success. US fuel prices, which surged after the start of the Iran war, piling pressure on Americans’ cost of living, “will soon come plummeting down”, he claimed in a social media post.

“We’re celebrating the greatest oil victory in history,” he said at the rally, pointing out the ship off the Texan coast. “The oil provided is being provided to the United States at zero cost to the American taxpayer.”

Moments before Trump took the stage in Texas, he claimed on his Truth Social platform: “By unleashing Energy Dominance from Alaska, all the way down to Venezuela, I have made the Western Hemisphere the Energy Capital of the World.”

The deal has also drawn skepticism as critics complained that the Trump administration has not pushed a transition to democracy in Venezuela, were elections have not been held since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence.

The urgency of the oil agreement stems from Trump’s opting into the war with Iran in February. Gas prices have shot up nationwide after Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies.

articles.title: PNP orders tighter watch on recruiters targeting Filipinos for military work
articles.summary: The PNP is stepping up surveillance of suspected illegal recruiters offering Filipinos high-paying military jobs abroad.

blocks.text: October 28, 2026 | 7:00am
Phi­lippine National Police (PNP) Chief PLtGen. Jose Melencio Nartatez, Jr.
Philippine National Police / Facebook page

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) has ordered tighter monitoring of suspected illegal recruitment schemes targeting Filipinos seeking employment abroad, particularly military-related jobs in Eastern Euroipe.

In a statement on Tuesday, October 27, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. directed concerned police units to coordinate closely with relevant government agencies to come up with measures to protect Filipinos from dangerous overseas job offers.

"We will not allow unscrupulous individuals or syndicates to exploit the aspirations of any of our kababayan for overseas employment. No promise of a high-paying job should come at the expense of a Filipino's safety, dignity, or future," Nartatez said.
Nartatez also called for intensified surveillance and intelligence operations against deceptive recruitment networks.
The warning came amid reports that at least three Filipinos have died in the ongoing armed conflict between Ukraine and Russia.

"Illegal recruiters prey on the hopes of our kababayans by disguising dangerous schemes as opportunities for a better future. We will strengthen our intelligence operations and coordination with partner agencies to expose these schemes and hold those responsible accountable," Nartatez said.

Intercepted in Davao. The PNP's heightened vigilance follows the Bureau of Immigration's recent interception of three Filipinos at Davao International Airport before their scheduled departure on October 17.
The men were suspected of being recruited for military and border guard positions in Eastern Europe.
During initial questioning, the travelers claimed they were heading to Thailand to participate in or coach a Muay Thai tournament.
However, they later disclosed that they intended to proceed to Eastern Europe for work and had allegedly been promised monthly salaries of P200,000.
According to the men, two foreign recruiters offered to shoulder their travel expenses and arrange their European electronic visas while they were in Thailand.
The group was initially instructed on October 13 to take a supposed "backdoor" route through Zamboanga before the recruiters changed the plan to air travel through Davao.
Following their interception, the three were referred to the Inter-Agency Council Against Trafficking for further investigation and assistance.

articles.title: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape
articles.summary: Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing

blocks.text: The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.

In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls, the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.

The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, currently projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.

The exit polls gave a narrow lead to Eisenkot’s opposition bloc over Netanyahu’s governing coalition and its supporters, though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party.

If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely lengthy process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role.

Eisenkot will argue that he commands the bigger overall bloc and has the better chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).

They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben Gvir in this election”.

However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.

Negotiations with the Joint List, with 10 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinians Israeli citizens, who are currently exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.
“Laying down conditions won’t work with the Joint List,” Shbita said. “We will negotiate as equals because we need each other.”

In the absence of an agreement with one or both of the Palestinian groupings, it is possible that Eisenkot could try to govern as a minority government, with informal vote-by-vote agreements that would keep the new coalition afloat.

It would be an unstable solution, making another election more than likely. That would provide Netanyahu the opportunity to rally support among conservative Israeli Jews and claim to have been vindicated in his campaign slogan, “the Right or Palestine” (which rhymes in Hebrew).

Netanyahu has looked beaten before over his three decades at or near the top, and staged a comeback each time with the aid of his unparalleled tactical skills as a dealmaker. No one is yet ruling out another breathtaking political escape but this time, if he does bounce back, he would owe his resurrection to his avowed political enemies for dropping him a lifeline rather than make historic compromises across Israel’s deep racial divide.

articles.title: 'Puppy angel on earth': B.C. man killed while on volunteer animal rescue mission in Ukraine
articles.summary: Jesse Adams from Sooke, B.C., was killed while rescuing animals with Animal Rescue Kharkiv. His friends and colleagues remember him as a compassionate and kind person who loved animals.

image.caption: Vancouver Islander Jesse Adams was killed Sunday in a drone attack in Ukraine, according to Ukraine-based group Animal Rescue Kharkiv. (Jesse Adams/Facebook)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
Jesse Adams from Sooke, B.C., was killed while rescuing animals with Animal Rescue Kharkiv. His friends and colleagues remember him as a compassionate and kind person who loved animals.
Jesse Adams was killed Sunday in a drone attack, according to Ukraine-based group
B.C.'s animal rescue community is grieving the death of a Sooke man who was killed in Ukraine Sunday.
Jesse Adams, co-founder of RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, was evacuating animals from Kramatorsk, a city in eastern Ukraine, when he was killed, according to Animal Rescue Kharkiv (ARK).
"An enemy FPV [first-person view] drone attacked our vehicle, which had just been loaded with rescued animals," ARK said in a post on Facebook.
Adams, who volunteered with ARK as an animal rescue mission worker, was severely injured and taken to a local hospital.
"Tragically, despite their best efforts, they were unable to save his life," ARK said.
Jesse Adams is seen at RainCoast Dog Rescue Society in 2021. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)
The organization said Adams had rescued hundreds of animals with them, calling him kind and compassionate.
"When someone travels halfway around the world and chooses to work beside you in some of the most difficult conditions, it means more than words can say."

items: This B.C. man was rejected from military service in Ukraine. Now, he's saving pets hurt and abandoned by war

blocks.text: Langford resident Chadalee Howie got her dog Winston from Adams in 2024, and said he was an amazing, kind-hearted person.
"He's like a puppy angel on earth."
She said Adams paid for the first bag of puppy food and gave her a gift certificate for groceries.
"To just run away to one of the world's most dangerous places and start rescuing animals, that's who he is."
Adams is seen in 2018 with one of the cats at the rescue. He was in Ukraine rescuing animals. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)
Penny Stone, executive director of the Victoria Humane Society, said Adams was a "go-to guy" if they needed help.
"There was no animal too small, too big, too scary, too aggressive," Stone said.
Even while in Ukraine, Adams was still doing adoptions and taking calls for RainCoast, Stone said.
"He loved animals, but he also loved people," she said.
"He'll be remembered as an animal rescuer, but he certainly had a lot more good qualities than just that."
Adams was remembered for rescuing a large number of animals on Vancouver Island and in Ukraine. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)
Emma Hamill, regional manager of animal care services for the B.C. SPCA who worked with Adams in Victoria, described him as collaborative and open-minded.
She said he had a gift for reaching vulnerable people, particularly in remote areas where larger organizations can be limited.
"His power to build relationships and help people and animals together was such a big piece of his legacy," Hamill said.
Rescues with international reach
Lori Kalef, director of programs for SPCA International and Adams' longtime friend, said she first met him in 2013 when rescuing a dog from Iraq.
"The dog was very, very difficult and had behavioural issues, so I was given Jesse's name right away," Kalef said.
Two hours later, Kalef said, he showed up and said, "no problem."
He adopted the dog and called him Teddy, Kalef said.
She said Adams worked in rescues all over the world and at home.
Jesse Adams is seen with Lori Kalef of the SPCA in this image. (Submitted by Lori Kalef)
Kalef added that he was instrumental in helping evacuate almost 300 dogs and cats from Afghanistan in 2021 when the government collapsed and the Taliban took over.
Kalef said Adams connected various groups and planned a temporary makeshift shelter for the animals at Vancouver International Airport.

items: Planeload of abandoned dogs and cats from Afghanistan arrives in Vancouver

blocks.text: Once Adams started working, Kalef said, there was no turning back.
"Every single animal was 'muffin' or 'sweetheart.' Every single dog that was blind or deaf, he handled with the utmost love, like they were his animals."
RainCoast helped find homes for most of the dogs rescued from Afghanistan, Kalef said.
"He had a footprint — and a pawprint — in so many areas in the world."
'My privilege': Adams on his work
On Oct. 20, Adams shared a message on his Instagram account describing his travels to the "frontline city of Kramatorsk in Eastern Ukraine."
He said the group helped evacuate 80 dogs and cats.

items: A week after war broke out in Ukraine, these volunteers started to rescue pets trapped in apartments

blocks.text: "These poor animals do not understand war and are simply innocent victims of another country invading Ukraine," wrote Adams last Tuesday. "Each day more and more innocent civilians and animals are injured or killed by drones, bombs, and missile attacks."

"It breaks my heart that we even have to do this type of work, but it is my privilege and honor to be a small part of helping these animals reach a better life for themselves and their families, or to be adopted into new families."
Stone said Adams died a hero and "doing what he loved to do."
With files from Isabella Calissi and Cory Correia

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US amid investigation
articles.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost to incumbent Lula in Sunday's presidential election, has reportedly fled the country. Bolsonaro, who is facing multiple corruption probes, has refused to concede.

image.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro is believed to be en route to the USImage: Eraldo Peres/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the United States after he was defeated in Sunday's presidential election.
The US State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the US, a senior State Department official said.

Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured the runoff victory in elections, told supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had left the country.
Brazil is "the second country" of the Bolsonaro family, Lula added.
"The first is licking American boots," the reelected president said. "Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow who secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something."
Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results
Bolsonaro leaves Brazil after losing presidential election: What to know
The Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to stop him from leaving the country. The senator is facing multiple corruption investigations.
Bolsonaro said that he had received the Supreme Court order outside the home where his father, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest.
He said Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the order, the same judge who sentenced his father to prison.

The senator said in an Instagram post on Monday that he had planned to hand over his passports, but reports on Tuesday said the passports had been canceled after the deadline to turn them in had passed.
Bolsonaro lost the election runoff on Sunday after an incredibly tight voting count through the evening until Lula surged ahead.
The leftist incumbent eventually won by a clear margin of more than 4 million votes.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election results, pointing to the evening extension of voting past the planned closing time of 5 p.m. across the country.
Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results, but the senator has not yet conceded victory.
His refusal to accept the results mirrors how his father Jair disputed his election defeat to Lula four years ago.
Jair is serving a more than 20-year prison sentence for plotting a coup to overthrow Lula after the 2022 election.
How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?
The Argentinian Migration Department on Wednesday said Flavio Bolsonaro and his family had briefly entered Argentina before taking a private plane to Ecuador.
The department added that Bolsonaro and his family had entered the country through the Tancredo ​Neves International ‌Bridge border crossing in ​Misiones ⁠Province.
It also said that they were holding valid travel documents and that there was "no legal impediment" blocking their entry, despite a court order banning Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil.
Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.
Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts were unclear, with some reports claiming that he had landed in the US, while others said he was in Ecuador or still en route.
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday that he "would approve" of the far-right senator coming to the US.
"I think they're fine people. The election was very strange, and I ‌thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint ⁠Base ⁠Andrews.
Trump also repeated his belief that Flavio's father, Jair, was the victim of persecution by Brazil's judicial authorities.
"The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn't involved," Trump added. "That's Brazil. It's a different country."
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.
Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro reportedly entered Argentina through this border crossingImage: Christian Rizzi/AFP

blocks.text: What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?
The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was taken from government pensions for senior citizens.
A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."
Bolsonaro will lose his immunity from prosecution once his senate term ends in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

articles.title: Serial killer Ted Bundy linked through DNA to 1974 murder of Utah girl
articles.summary:
Discovery comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed that Bundy had killed another Utah girl that year

The notorious serial killer Ted Bundy has been found responsible, through DNA…

blocks.text: The notorious serial killer Ted Bundy has been found responsible, through DNA evidence, for the murder of Melissa Ann Smith, a 17-year-old Utah girl who went missing in 1974 before her nude body was found days later, state authorities announced at a Tuesday news conference.
The breakthrough comes months after Utah county detectives confirmed in April that Bundy killed another Utah girl, 17-year-old Laura Ann Aime, in 1974.
Bundy had confessed to killing Laura during a string of admissions he made before being executed in 1989 for two of his murders.
Laura was last seen during a Halloween party, before being found dead and severely beaten in late November 1974.
It was not until this year, though, that new DNA testing backed Bundy’s account.
Bodily fluid extracted from Laura’s body was a match to Bundy’s known DNA profile, law enforcement officials said then.
That discovery put into motion the closure of Smith’s homicide investigation.
The Y-STR DNA profile recovered from Laura’s body was a genetic match to one found from Melissa’s body.

“This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence, even when decades have passed,” said Salt Lake county sheriff Rosie Rivera on Tuesday. “We have the ability to take a look at these cases again and again.”
Between 1974 and 1978, Bundy went on a violent rampage, sexually assaulting and killing at least 30 women across the American west and Florida.

“The voices and cherished memories of Melissa Ann Smith and Laura Ann Aime and others involved in these cases ring louder than the hate and sedition of the one that took their lives,” said Mike Reynolds, a sergeant with the Utah county sheriff’s office sergeant on Tuesday. “With every case closure may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out.”

articles.title: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare
articles.summary: As the US president casts doubt on the security of the midterm elections, BBC Verify examines his claims.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
President Donald Trump has offered a $1m (£750,000) reward to people who report cases of voter fraud in the US which lead to a conviction.
Ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, Trump has been casting doubt on the security of the vote - alleging "rampant" cheating in postal voting and non-citizens voting.
However, studies suggest actual cases of these are extremely rare.
BBC Verify has taken a look at the evidence and Trump's proposed changes to the voting system.
How has Trump tried to change postal voting?
For years, Trump has made repeated unsubstantiated claims that postal voting leads to widespread fraud.
He has also encouraged Republicans to vote by mail in the midterms and has said he has cast his ballot by post in the past.
The president has been unsuccessful in his push for Congress to pass an act which would only allow people to vote by mail if they are disabled, ill, serving in the military, or travelling.
The majority of states allow, external people to vote by mail without having to provide a reason, and in the 2024 presidential election about 48 million people cast postal ballots.

Trump signed an executive order last year which directed the US Postal Service to only deliver ballots to voters on lists of citizens compiled by government agencies. It also sought to require states to use the same envelope style for postal votes.

items: What is the SAVE America Act and what would it do?
Trump criticises Supreme Court after justices block mail-in ballot restrictions

blocks.text: However, the order was rejected by the US Supreme Court which called such changes so close to the midterm elections "arbitrary and capricious" - but said it could revisit the issue afterwards.

US states have different rules for verifying postal ballots, but every state matches certain voter information on the ballots against what they have on file to check they are eligible and most also conduct signature checks, external.
What does the evidence show on postal voting fraud?
Studies of multiple US elections suggest postal vote fraud has been extremely rare.
The Brookings Institute policy research think tank, external looked at the 2016, 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections and found an average of about four cases of fraud out of every 10 million postal votes.
The report used a database kept by the Heritage Foundation - a think tank which has been aligned with Trump in the past - which records cases of electoral fraud that have ended in a conviction.
We looked back in the database, external over the last 20 years and found it has tallied 325 convictions as a result of the fraudulent use of postal ballots.

A 2020 study by the American Statistical Association, external looked at cases of voter fraud in eight states which send postal ballots to all eligible voters and found no evidence that voting by mail increased the risk of voter fraud overall.
For example, according to the study, Oregon recorded 40 fraud cases between 2000 and 2020 having sent out more than 100 million postal ballots over that period.
How has Trump tried to change voter ID rules?
Trump has claimed non-citizen voting is widespread, and prior to the 2024 election he said Democrats were allowing millions of migrants into the US "so they can vote, vote, vote".
It is illegal for non-citizens to vote in US federal elections - punishments can include a prison sentence, a fine, and deportation.

The voting act the president has pushed Congress to pass would require voters to show a government-issued photo identification before they cast their ballots, as well as proof of citizenship when registering to vote and ongoing citizenship verification.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Millions of people have already voted early in the US midterm elections

blocks.text: Millions of people have already voted early in the US midterm elections
Critics have raised concerns that stricter voter ID requirements could harm voter turnout as people may not have a passport or the required government-issued photo ID.

"We don't have a national ID card that the government gives out, unlike a lot of countries. Drivers licence is most common but it doesn't identify your immigration status so the ID that most Americans carry around wouldn't be enough for you to vote," says Jonathan Diaz, a voting rights expert at the Campaign Legal Center.

items: Can illegal immigrants really vote in the US election?

blocks.text: A 2023 survey by the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external suggested that about 21.3 million voting-age American citizens, or about 9%, do not have documents proving citizenship readily available.
However, others argue that there has been no noticeable impact from existing voter ID laws.

"When scholars look at the effect of voter ID laws - either what the conservatives say on fraud or what progressive groups warn against about voter suppression - there doesn't seem to be a lot of proof that either has happened," says Walter Olson, an election expert at the conservative Cato Institute.

A number of largely Republican-run states have tightened voter ID requirements in the last couple of years. There have been 21 restrictive voting laws enacted since the 2024 election to establish stricter ID requirements, according to a study by the Brennan Center for Justice, external.
What does the evidence show on non-citizens voting?
Multiple studies show proven instances of non-citizens voting in past US elections have been very small.
The Heritage Foundation's database identified 24 cases of non-citizens being convicted for voting between 2005 and 2025.

A 2026 analysis by Reuters, external of non-citizen voting cases brought in federal courts found that over the last 30 years 129 people have been criminally charged and 73 of those cases resulted in a conviction.

"The fact that it's illegal for non-citizens to vote is a pretty strong deterrent in the first place as many worry about their immigration status and it would be an extremely risky move to vote," says Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institute.
"There's never been any evidence that there are many people who have done that, certainly not enough to influence an election."
What about non-citizens registered on voter rolls?

Trump has also pushed for states to use a federal database - the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save) database - to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens and remove them from voter rolls.

The tool has access to information about naturalised citizens and non-citizens who have contacted the federal government previously. It was launched in the 1980s to help government agencies verify individuals' eligibility for government benefits based on their immigration status.

Critics have questioned the reliability of using the data to remove people from voter rolls as they say it could be outdated and include people who have since become US citizens - but the US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using it this way.

items: US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship

blocks.caption: Image caption, Every US state allows some postal voting and 29% of voters cast a ballot that way in the 2024 presidential election

blocks.text: Every US state allows some postal voting and 29% of voters cast a ballot that way in the 2024 presidential election

"Federal databases can be invaluable to states trying to update their voter rolls so long as their limitations are understood," says Olson. "So part of the Trump plan which requires the sharing of information is positive, even if the second part to require states to treat the database contents as reliable despite their continuing evident gaps and inaccuracies is bad."
The use of the programme by individual states is voluntary, and from those who have used it recently the number of non-citizens detected has been small.
In Georgia, after an audit of the state's voter rolls, 432 possible non-citizens were identified, external on its voter rolls over 30 years.

The Department of Homeland Security provided Nevada with a list of 185 names which it claimed identified non-citizens who had been improperly allowed to register to vote, but state officials found that they were all in fact citizens., external

The White House has pointed to a case in New Jersey, where this summer a software glitch in the state's drivers licensing department registered about 6,600 non-citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024. State officials have said fewer than 400 cast ballots and they have all now been removed from the system.

The US Justice Department requested that California doesn't count 20,000 postal ballots ahead of the midterms from people it claims are "likely non-citizen registrants" - but that request has been rejected by an appeals court.
Out of that 20,000, it has charged 28 people, external who the department says are non-citizens who had illegally registered to vote.

articles.title: Ex-wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president freed after collapse of attempted murder case
articles.summary: Marry Mubaiwa had been held on remand for seven years after being charged in 2019 for her then husband's attempted murder.

blocks.text: The former wife of Zimbabwe's vice-president has been freed from remand after seven years while on trial for his attempted murder.
Marry Mubaiwa was charged in 2019, after her then husband Gen Constantino Chiwenga accused her of trying to impede his medical treatment in South Africa.
Ordering her release, a magistrate said Mubaiwa had suffered mental, physical and financial prejudice during the trial, state-owned daily the Herald said.
The ruling was made after the state asked for the trial to be postponed by a month in order to engage witnesses.
Her lawyer described the ruling as a victory that had come too late, because her client's rights had been violated by the delay in the trial.
Speaking outside court in the capital Harare on Tuesday, the lawyer added that if the state moved for a new trial, they would deal with it when it happened.
Mubaiwa was accused of attempting to kill Chiwenga, while he was in hospital in Pretoria. The vice-president then went to China for four months of treatment.
Mubaiwa was remanded in custody and denied bail.
According to the New Zimbabwe news website, Mubaiwa celebrated her release outside court, and said justice had been achieved and that she was proud of her lawyer.
In 2017, Chiwenga played a key role in overthrowing then President Robert Mugabe.

articles.title: Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
articles.summary: Early indications suggest it will be some time before the shape of new government and who will lead it is clear
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv Julian Borger in Jerusalem and Peter Beaumont

blocks.text: Israel’s election was too close to call on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters.

Exit polls published on Tuesday evening, they suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party.
The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called.

After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis.

The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition.

The exit polls – if they prove accurate – suggest a struggle for either Likud or Eisenkot’s Yashar to find a road to a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Likud’s projected showing, not for the first time, appears to have defied predictions in the runup to the vote.
What is clear, however, is that Netanayhu no longer has a claim to a mandate with his political fate in the balance.

The exit polls were released after a last-ditch effort by Netanyahu and several other parties to keep polling stations open beyond their 10pm deadline was rejected by the Central Elections Committee as the prime minister suggested publicly that efforts were being made by the “left and Arabs” to steal the election, a claim rejected by the committee that said it had seen no evidence of systematic tampering.
Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.

Tuesday’s election, which drew the highest turnout in 50 years, had been framed as a referendum on nearly 17 years of unbroken rule by Benjamin Netanyahu, who has most recently overseen three years of unprecedented conflict, instability and growing international isolation.

With more than 7 million people eligible to vote, by 6pm voter turnout was 74.3% – a rise of about 9% on the previous election – with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting. There were also reports of tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad who had arrived to vote in recent days, with many still arriving at Ben Gurion airport to cast their ballots on Tuesday.

Voting was heavy in a number of major cities, including Tel Aviv and Haifa, which some analysts had suggested would benefit the opposition, with long queues to vote in some locations. That pattern was repeated in Israeli-Arab towns, many of which have a long history of boycotting elections.

blocks.caption: Israeli-Arab voters arrive to cast their ballots at a polling station in Nazareth. Photograph: Adri Salido/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: As polls opened on Tuesday, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition allies launched what critics condemned as a scare campaign to encourage their supporters to turn out, with the familiar racist tactic of warning that large numbers of Israeli Arabs would be voting. Netanyahu made a similar claim to rally support in 2015.

In a recorded message to voters, Netanyahu suggested Arabs and the left were trying to steal the election and Likud claimed suspected irregularities at hundreds of polling stations used by Israeli Arabs.
Israeli citizens of Palestinian origin make up about 20% of the country’s population.
That prompted Netanyahu’s main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, to say Netanyahu was laying the ground to challenge the result.

blocks.caption: A Likud election poster at a polling station in Jerusalem. Photograph: Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Netanyahu has returned to his familiar tricks, lies and fearmongering to mobilise voters,” he said. “The same lies we saw in previous election campaigns.”

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023 – an event that many blamed on Netanyahu’s failings – Israel has devastated Gaza with the loss of more than 74,000 Palestinian lives, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.

Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners have also attracted international opprobrium for Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank, where violent Jewish settlers have been accused of pogroms against Palestinians and ethnic cleansing.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian family walk past campaign posters for Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, in Beit Kahil in the West Bank. Photograph: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Despite the many issues confronting the country, much of the focus in the campaign has been on the contrasting characters of the two main party leaders – the machiavellian, grandstanding Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption, against Eisenkot, the unpolished former IDF chief of staff who rose from humble origins.
The campaign, unusually febrile even by Israeli standards, included a struggling Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

On Tuesday, encouraging ultra-orthodox voters, Netanyahu – who has long elided his personal and political survival with that of Israel – returned to his apocalyptic language. “The Jewish state is on the brink of ruin,” he said.

In the midst of a major trial for corruption, which has been moving at a glacial pace through the courts, Netanyahu has appeared rattled by the challenge mounted against him by an array of centre-right parties whose unifying pitch has been “anyone but Netanyahu”.

“This is a very moving and fateful moment,” he told journalists after voting, saying he believed the Arab parties that could make or break the election were “receiving massive, truly massive, support ... heading to the polls in unprecedented numbers”.

Despite tonight’s results, the complexity of Israel’s fragmented political system, with many parties jostling and horse trading, means that it will probably be some time before the shape of any future government – and who will lead it – is clear.
All of which has amplified the importance of Israeli Arab parties, which could emerge as potential kingmakers.
“Our vote will change the government,” the head of the Islamist Ra’am party, Mansour Abbas, said while voting, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.

Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for taunting Palestinian detainees and saying some Palestinians in Gaza are “not even people”, said “it will be Mansour Abbas’s government” if Netanyahu and his allies lose.
Underlining the sense of a country at a defining crossroads, an editorial in the left-leaning Haaretz publication had exhorted Israelis to vote which they did in huge numbers.

“Israel cannot afford another four years under Netanyahu,” it said. “It has exhausted its reserves. The erosion of its diplomatic credit has reached dangerous proportions, and its tired citizens are at the very limits of what they can bear.”

articles.title: Alexander brothers each sentenced to 30 years in prison for sex trafficking case
articles.summary: The three brothers were found guilty of drugging and raping several women over the course of decades.

blocks.text: Three brothers - two of them wealthy real-estate moguls - were sentenced to 30 years each in prison for drugging and raping dozens of women over the course of decades.

Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, were found guilty in March of using their wealth and social status to lure women to parties and luxury homes, where they sexually assaulted them.

On Tuesday morning, the court in New York heard from 12 victims, including one who did not testify during the trial, about the psychological trauma they endured after the Alexander brothers raped them and their desire for the shame they had felt to instead fall on the defendants.
Many asked the judge to impose the maximum sentence of life in prison for each brother.
Maya Miller told the court that after Tal Alexander raped her in 2014, she lost all sense of safety.
"I carry a quiet funeral within me for the person I might've become if this never happened to me," she said.
Another victim, who went by the pseudoym Isa Brooks, said after being raped by Tal and Alon Alexander when she was 16 years old, she lost the ability to trust herself.
"I had no idea the danger I was in til it was too late," she said.
Another woman said that when she planned to come forward about being raped, Tal Alexander threatened that he knew where her sister worked.

During the women's speeches, the three Alexander brothers showed little emotion. They stared ahead or conferred with their lawyers, who said they had advised their clients not to look at the victims while they spoke so it wasn't misconstrued as staring.
Prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa said the brothers deserved the maximum punishment for their crimes, saying the facts of the case "paint a truly devastating picture".
"For years, they honed their methods of luring women with the promise of luxury," she said, adding that they were "completely unmoved by the path of suffering they left behind them."

During the five-week trial, 11 women - including several who said they were minors at the time of the assaults - testified that the brothers gave them gifts and flew them to locations including Aspen and the Bahamas where they fed them drugs before raping them.
Prosecutors said the brothers' pattern of abusive behaviour began in high school, though the trial covered their crimes starting in 2008.

They had accused the three of slipping drugs in women's drinks, and said they "physically restrained and held down their victims during the rapes and sexual assaults and ignored screams and explicit requests to stop".
Lawyers for the brothers had argued the sex was consensual and that they were womanizers, but not sexual abusers. They pushedd for the lowest possible sentence for the brothers, 15 years.
Two of the brothers, Tal and Oren, made their wealth from selling luxury properties in New York and Miami.

They worked for American real estate giant Douglas Elliman, selling properties for celebrities including Lindsay Lohan, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West. In 2022, they founded their own New York-based firm called Official. Alon worked at the family's private security firm, Kent Security.
As they heard their sentences, the brotehrs did not react or show emotion, staring straight ahead.

articles.title: What we know about Ukraine-Russia truce in Oleshky, brokered by Melania Trump
articles.summary: The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has had no electricity, gas or water for three years, as residents reported having to eat weeds to survive.

blocks.text: Fighting in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has stopped after a truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady.
The truce is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation on Friday.
But residents have told the BBC they were weary of the ceasefire as the evacuation routes could potentially take them through Crimea and Russia.
BBC's Ukraine correspondent, Dan Johnson, has more details.

articles.title: Olivia Chow elected as Toronto mayor for second term in victory for progressives
articles.summary:
Tightly fought election saw record turnout as incumbent mayor ran against her rival Brad Bradford

The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and…

blocks.text: The mayor of Toronto, Olivia Chow, promised more rental housing, free school lunches and reduce fares for frequent transit riders after she was elected to a decisive second term as mayor in a wave of support for progressives councillors.

The tightly fought election saw record turnout but Chow ultimately turned in a dominant 13 percentage point win over her rival, Brad Bradford, receiving 54% of the vote compared to Bradford’s 41%. Many had been expecting a far closer race, given weeks of polling that suggested a dead heat between the pair who presented differing visions for Canada’s largest city.

Chow bet that voters would accept her policies to confront a mounting affordability crisis that has engulfed major cities around the world. Her win also signals voters see that progressive urban politics can resist cost-of-living backlash that has toppled over governments.
On Monday night, Chow thanked her supporters and Bradford.

“I know we share a love for Toronto and a belief in its future,” she told a jubilant crowd. “We can disagree on how we get there, or what it looks like, but I do not doubt we both want what is best for our city.”

Chow, 69, has long been a fixture of the city’s politics. She previously served as a school board trustee, city councillor and federal member of parliament. Her total of more than 532,000 votes nearly doubles what she received in 2023.

Bradford, a former city councillor and urban planner, spent much of the campaign focusing on what he said was Chow’s failure to stem the rising cost of living and to address crime. He told residents crime was so bad in Toronto that he slept with a baseball bat next to his bed.
While auto theft and high-value property crime have risen, most other categories – including homicides, firearms related violence and assault – have all dropped significantly in recent years.
Bradford said more police were needed, and pledged to cut taxes and city spending.

In a city that has experienced antisemitic vandalism and shootings at Jewish schools, Bradford aimed to ally himself with Toronto’s Jewish community, and said that Chow’s decision not to attend a debate on antisemitism meant she wouldn’t be an effective voice to combat hate. For her part, Chow increased the size of the police department’s hate crimes unit and pushed a “bubble zone” bylaw that barred protest within 50 meters of places of worship, schools, childcare centers other vulnerable institutions.

In his concession speech, the 40-year-old took a conciliatory tone. “I want her to succeed. And my supporters and the nearly 400,000 people that cast a vote for us tonight, they want her to succeed too,” he said. “We all love this city. We know it can be better.”
Bradford also acknowledged the daunting odds against his candidacy: no incumbent mayor who has sought re-election in Canada’s largest city has ever lost.

Chow also benefited from her apparent ability to manage a fraught political relationship with the Ontario government and its premier, Doug Ford. When she was first elected in 2023, Ford said she would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city. While Ford did not endorse her in this election, he told reporters the pair had a “phenomenal relationship” and said people should “read between the lines” when it comes to his preferred candidate. However, the two are likely to spar in a fierce battle over the city’s bike lanes.

Like other major urban centers, Toronto remains locked in a battle over affordability, an issue that is expected to remain a challenge for the incoming council, where a large number of progressive candidates both returned and won for the first time, including Diana McNally Chan, a well-known advocate for unhoused people, who will be the first renter to sit on city council.

articles.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
articles.summary: The truce was originally planned for the stranded residents of Oleshky, and Russia and Ukraine say no breaches have been reported.
articles.byline: Paul Kirby, Olga Malchevska, Dan Johnson

blocks.text: A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.
However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.
US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

That was later corroborated by the press secretary to Ukraine's public ombudsman, and by Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of Kherson, who said Russian shelling had stopped both in Kherson city, which is in Ukrainian hands, and the wider region.
Under the deal, the ceasefire will be followed by deliveries of humanitarian aid to Oleshky and then evacuations, planned for Friday, for anyone wishing to leave.
An estimated 1,700 to 2,000 people remain in Oleshky itself and a few thousand more in surrounding areas.
Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.

Both sides said the ceasefire was being observed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said everything was proceeding "according to plan", and paid tribute to US mediation and in particular representatives of Melania Trump.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said if the ceasefire produced results, it could "pave the way for other steps in the peace process".

A key official in President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary party, David Arakhamia, said it would continue until 22:59 Ukrainian time on Sunday 1 November, and described the truce as the "largest de-escalation since 2022".
Before the war Oleshky was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka Dam was blown up in 2023, flooding the area and killing many people in Oleshky itself.

Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escaping is too risky because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.

One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a landmine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations: "I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.

Pope Leo appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.
Then the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.
On Tuesday, the US first lady said on X that the area covered by the ceasefire "has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys".

The current truce is supposed to enable roads to be cleared of mines for supplies to get into the city possibly on Thursday, and for residents to have safe passage out in an evacuation planned for Friday.

Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices".

Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, and residents are wary of trusting officials with their names and addresses. However, a local volunteer told the BBC that about 500 people had already expressed interest by Tuesday afternoon.

Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-installed head of occupied areas of Kherson, said temporary accommodation had been prepared in the region itself as well as Russian-annexed Crimea and across the Russian border in the Rostov, Krasnodar and Stavropol regions.
Saldo told Russian media that most Oleshky residents wanted to leave the city and stay in Russia, although his account has not been corroborated on the ground.
Zelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there".
He said some residents would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and that ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.

One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky through minefields around three weeks ago, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus. He called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".
However, bridges across the River Dnipro have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous, so crossing into Ukrainian-controlled territory appears impossible.

Across the river, in Kherson city, no explosions have been heard and no drone-related injuries reported since 03:00 (01:00 GMT) on Tuesday and cars and pedestrians have been moving freely, according to local reports.
"Judging from the fact that more people are walking around, it feels a bit calmer," Galina Kyrychenko, a resident in the city, told public broadcaster Suspilne.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv.

articles.title: Politics live: Greens propose tax change to save Australians $1,000 a year; eSafety says social media akin to gladiator arena
articles.summary: • Get our breaking news email, free app or

blocks.text: Shoebridge to pitch increased welfare spending, hike in tax-free threshold

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, will address the National Press Club in Canberra today, promising to help Australians struggling with cost-of-living and answering questions about allegations against senator Jordon Steele-John.

He will propose lifting the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000, meaning people earning a wage won’t pay tax on their first $26,000. He says that will save the average working Australian more than $1,000.
The Greens are also proposing a $1,000 annual boost for people on income support, including pensioners, carers, students, and job seekers.
double quotation markNo matter who you are, whether you’re working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you’ll get more than $1,000.

Costings for the Greens from the Parliamentary Budget Office show the plan would cost about $22bn a year, with Shoebridge proposing to pay for it through higher taxes on gas exports and a market-based tax on resources companies.
Steele-John is on leave from parliament amid an investigation into allegations about his conduct towards women. He has denied the allegations.

blocks.caption: Greens senator David Shoebridge. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
